Solution.why: Executes the skeleton with correct syntax, ensuring the person with the most friends is returned with their friend count.

Solution.intuition: The final query is the exact code that solves the problem as described.

Problem.why: Defines the input table and the required output (id and type) for tree node classification.

Approach.what_if: If you check leaf before root, a single-node tree would be mislabeled as leaf instead of root.
Approach.intuition: Like sorting mail: first find the top boss (root), then find employees with no reports (leaves).

Pattern.why: Uses a CASE expression with a subquery or LEFT JOIN to check if a node's id appears as a parent.
Pattern.what_if: Without this pattern, you'd have no way to know which nodes have children, leading to wrong leaf/inner labels.
Pattern.intuition: It's like checking a directory: a folder is a leaf if no other folder lists it as parent.

Skeleton.why: Provides the basic SQL structure: SELECT id, CASE ... END AS type FROM Tree ORDER BY id.

Skeleton.intuition: The skeleton is the empty house; we just need to fill in the CASE logic.

Solution.intuition: The final code is the recipe: first check for root, then check for leaf by seeing if the id is ever a parent, otherwise it's inner.

Problem.why: Defines the input (three side lengths per row) and the output (a 'Yes'/'No' column indicating triangle validity).

Pattern.why: This is a straightforward conditional check per row, often implemented with a CASE WHEN or IF statement in SQL.
Pattern.what_if: Using a wrong pattern (e.g., checking only one inequality) would produce incorrect results.
Pattern.intuition: For each row, just apply the three conditions and output 'Yes' if all hold, else 'No'.

Solution.what_if: If you skip saving next, you lose the rest of the list after redirecting curr.next.
Solution.intuition: Snap the arrow backward, then step forward so you can snap the next arrow.

Problem.why: Defines the exact task: detect a cycle in a singly linked list.
Problem.what_if: Without a clear problem statement, you might solve the wrong variant or miss edge cases.

Approach.why: Floyd's algorithm uses two pointers moving at different speeds to detect cycles without extra memory.
Approach.what_if: Using a hash set would work but requires O(n) extra space, violating the constant space constraint.
Approach.intuition: Like two runners on a circular track: the faster one will eventually lap the slower one if the track is a loop.

Pattern.why: The fast pointer moves two steps per iteration, the slow pointer moves one step.
Pattern.what_if: If both moved at the same speed, they would never meet in a cycle unless starting at the same node.
Pattern.intuition: The relative speed difference ensures that if a cycle exists, the fast pointer will catch up to the slow one.

Skeleton.why: Initialize both pointers at the head, then loop while fast and fast.next are not null.
Skeleton.what_if: Forgetting to check fast.next could cause a null pointer exception when fast is at the last node.
Skeleton.intuition: The loop condition ensures we stop when the fast pointer reaches the end (no cycle) or when pointers meet (cycle).

Solution.why: Return true if slow equals fast (cycle detected), else false after loop ends.
Solution.what_if: Returning false prematurely or missing the equality check would give incorrect results.
Solution.intuition: If they meet, it's a cycle; if fast hits null, it's a straight line.

Pattern.what_if: Using top-down would require passing depth as a parameter, losing the elegant base-case simplicity.
Pattern.intuition: Leaves return 1, then each parent adds 1 to the max of its children's returns.

Skeleton.why: The base case (None → 0) stops recursion and handles empty subtrees correctly.

Problem.why: Defines the exact condition for two trees to be considered the same.

Approach.why: Recursion naturally mirrors the tree's hierarchical structure.
Approach.what_if: An iterative approach would require manual stack management and lose the elegant symmetry.

Problem.why: Defines the goal: mirror the tree by swapping every node's left and right children.
Problem.what_if: Without a clear goal, you might swap only some nodes or misinterpret the output.
Problem.intuition: Think of flipping the tree horizontally like a mirror image.

Approach.what_if: If you skip nodes, parts of the tree remain unmirrored.
Approach.intuition: You need to touch every node to flip its two branches.

Pattern.why: Recursion naturally handles the tree structure by processing subtrees independently.
Pattern.what_if: Without recursion, you'd need an explicit stack and risk complexity or errors.

Skeleton.why: Provides the base case (null node) and the recursive call structure.

Problem.why: Defines the exact output format (list of lists, level by level) that the solution must produce.

Approach.what_if: Using DFS without depth tracking would interleave nodes from different levels, breaking the level-by-level grouping.

Problem.why: Defines the exact condition every node must satisfy for the tree to be a valid BST.
Problem.what_if: Without a clear problem statement, you might accept a tree that only checks local parent-child relationships.
Problem.intuition: The problem is about enforcing global ordering constraints, not just local ones.

Skeleton.why: The skeleton provides the recursive function signature and base case (null node is valid).

Solution.why: The solution implements the recursive check: validate left with updated high, right with updated low.
Solution.what_if: If you skip updating the bounds correctly, you'll allow invalid subtrees to pass as valid.
Solution.intuition: Each recursive call tightens the range, ensuring every node is strictly between its ancestors' values.

Problem.why: Defines the goal: find the kth smallest value in a BST efficiently.
Problem.what_if: Without a clear problem statement, you might waste time sorting all values unnecessarily.
Problem.intuition: The BST property already orders values, so we just need to count during traversal.

Approach.why: Inorder traversal visits nodes in ascending order, directly giving the kth element.
Approach.what_if: Using a different traversal (e.g., preorder) would not yield sorted order, requiring extra sorting.

Pattern.why: Recursive or iterative inorder traversal with a counter tracks when we reach the kth node.

Solution.what_if: Returning the wrong value (e.g., the node itself) or not stopping early wastes time and memory.
Solution.intuition: The solution is like a countdown: when the counter hits zero, that's your answer.

Problem.why: Defines the exact goal: find the deepest node that is an ancestor of both p and q in a BST.
Problem.what_if: Without a clear problem statement, you might solve a different problem (e.g., LCA in a generic tree) and miss the BST optimization.
Problem.intuition: We need the node where the paths to p and q diverge.

Approach.why: Leverages BST property to decide direction without exploring both subtrees.
Approach.what_if: If you ignore BST ordering, you'd do a full tree traversal, wasting time and complexity.
Approach.intuition: If both nodes are smaller, go left; both larger, go right; otherwise, current node is the split point.

Pattern.why: This is a 'divide and conquer' pattern that prunes half the tree at each step.
Pattern.what_if: Skipping the pattern leads to O(n) instead of O(h) time, where h is tree height.
Pattern.intuition: It's like binary search on the tree structure.

Skeleton.why: Provides the iterative or recursive loop that moves through the tree based on comparisons.
Skeleton.what_if: Without a skeleton, you might write messy code that doesn't handle edge cases like p or q being the root.
Skeleton.intuition: Start at root, keep moving until the condition for split is met.

Solution.why: Implements the logic: while node exists, compare p and q values to node value, return node when split condition holds.
Solution.what_if: If the comparison logic is wrong (e.g., using < instead of <=), you might return a wrong ancestor or infinite loop.
Solution.intuition: The first node where p and q are on different sides (or one equals it) is the LCA.

Problem.why: Defines the exact condition: subRoot must appear as an identical subtree (structure and values) somewhere in root.
Problem.what_if: Misunderstanding the problem could lead to checking partial matches or ignoring value equality, yielding false positives.
Problem.intuition: We need to find a node in root whose entire tree (including all descendants) is exactly the same as subRoot.

Approach.why: Reuses a same-tree equality function at each node of root, recursively descending to check both children.
Approach.what_if: Without this recursive descent, we would only check the root node and miss subtrees deeper in the tree.
Approach.intuition: For every node in root, ask: 'Is this node's tree exactly subRoot?' If yes, return true; else check left and right children.

Pattern.why: Combines two recursive patterns: a helper to compare two trees (same-tree) and a traversal to check every node of root.
Pattern.what_if: Skipping the same-tree helper would require duplicating equality logic inside the main recursion, making the code messy and error-prone.
Pattern.intuition: We write a separate 'isSameTree' function and call it from the main 'isSubtree' function at each node.

Skeleton.why: Provides the structure: base cases for null nodes, then either same-tree match or recursive calls on left and right children.
Skeleton.what_if: If base cases are missing (e.g., not handling null root), the recursion may crash or produce incorrect results for empty trees.
Skeleton.intuition: If root is null, return false unless subRoot is also null (then true). Otherwise check equality or recurse on children.

Solution.why: Implements the recursive helper for same-tree and the main function that traverses root, returning the boolean result.
Solution.what_if: If the same-tree helper does not correctly check both structure and values, the subtree check will be unreliable.
Solution.intuition: The final code is a clean delegation: 'isSubtree' calls 'isSameTree' at each node, leveraging the helper's correctness.

Problem.why: Defines the input and output for reconstructing a unique binary tree from its preorder and inorder traversals.
Problem.what_if: Without clear problem definition, you might attempt to solve a different or ambiguous reconstruction task.
Problem.intuition: The problem is like using two different orderings of the same tree to figure out its original shape.

Approach.why: Leverages the fact that preorder's first element is the root, and inorder splits left and right subtrees.
Approach.what_if: Skipping this approach leads to inefficient brute-force or incorrect tree reconstruction.
Approach.intuition: The root is the first in preorder; its position in inorder tells you exactly how many nodes are on each side.

Pattern.why: Recursive divide-and-conquer on the two lists using the root's inorder index.
Pattern.what_if: Without recursion, you cannot systematically rebuild subtrees from the split lists.
Pattern.intuition: Each recursive call handles a smaller subtree by slicing both traversals based on the root's inorder position.

Skeleton.why: Defines the recursive function signature and base case (empty lists return None).
Skeleton.what_if: Missing base case causes infinite recursion or index errors.
Skeleton.intuition: The skeleton is the recursive shell that stops when there are no nodes left to process.

Solution.why: Builds a hashmap from inorder values to indices for O(1) lookups, then recursively constructs the tree.
Solution.what_if: Without the hashmap, each lookup would be O(n), making the overall solution O(n^2) instead of O(n).
Solution.intuition: The hashmap turns finding the root's position into a constant-time operation, making the recursion efficient.

Problem.why: Defines the goal: find the maximum sum of any contiguous path in a binary tree, where a path can start and end at any node.
Problem.what_if: Without this clear definition, you might incorrectly restrict paths to root-to-leaf or require the root to be included.
Problem.intuition: Think of the tree as a network of roads; you want the richest route between any two points, not just from the capital.

Approach.why: Use post-order DFS so each node can combine its left and right best downward sums to compute the best path through itself.
Approach.what_if: If you use pre-order or in-order, you'd lack the child results needed to evaluate paths that bend at the current node.
Approach.intuition: Like a manager collecting reports from both subordinates before deciding the team's best project.

Pattern.why: Each node returns the maximum sum of a downward path (only one child) to its parent, while a global variable tracks the best path that may go through both children.
Pattern.what_if: Returning the through-both-children sum upward would let the parent incorrectly reuse a path that already bends, breaking the tree structure.
Pattern.intuition: You can only hand one baton upward, but you can celebrate the best relay race that uses both arms.

Skeleton.why: Define a recursive function that returns the max downward sum from the current node, and update a global max with the candidate that includes both children.
Skeleton.what_if: Without the global variable, you'd lose the best path that doesn't go through the root, missing the answer.
Skeleton.intuition: The skeleton is a post-order traversal with a side pocket to stash the best find so far.

Solution.why: At each node, compute left_gain = max(0, dfs(left)), right_gain = max(0, dfs(right)), then update global max with node.val + left_gain + right_gain, and return node.val + max(left_gain, right_gain).
Solution.what_if: If you don't clamp negative gains to 0, you'd include branches that reduce the sum, making the path unnecessarily worse.
Solution.intuition: You can always choose to ignore a bad branch (like skipping a detour) to keep your path sum as high as possible.

Problem.why: Defines the input (k sorted linked lists) and output (one sorted list) to establish the goal.
Problem.what_if: Without a clear problem statement, you might solve the wrong task or miss constraints like 'sorted' and 'linked list'.
Problem.intuition: Think of merging k sorted lists like merging multiple sorted piles of cards into one sorted deck.

Approach.why: Using a min-heap avoids O(k) scans per node, reducing total complexity to O(N log k).
Approach.what_if: A naive approach (repeatedly scanning all k heads) would be O(Nk), which is too slow for large k.
Approach.intuition: The heap acts like a tournament where the smallest current head always wins the next pick.

Pattern.why: The min-heap pattern is standard for merging multiple sorted sequences efficiently.
Pattern.what_if: Skipping the heap pattern forces you to re-sort or merge pairwise, losing the log k advantage.
Pattern.intuition: It's like having a priority queue of the smallest remaining elements from each list.

Skeleton.why: A dummy head and a pointer simplify building the result list without special cases for the first node.
Skeleton.what_if: Without a dummy head, you'd need extra logic to handle the first node insertion, risking null pointer errors.
Skeleton.intuition: The dummy head is a placeholder that lets you always append via a single pointer.

Solution.why: Pushing each list's head into the heap, then repeatedly popping the smallest and pushing its next, builds the sorted output.
Solution.what_if: Forgetting the tie-breaking counter causes Python to crash when comparing ListNode objects with equal values.
Solution.intuition: Each pop gives the next smallest node; pushing its successor keeps the heap populated until all lists are exhausted.

Problem.why: Defines the goal: find the maximum sum of any contiguous subarray.
Problem.what_if: Without a clear problem statement, you might solve the wrong variant (e.g., non-contiguous).
Problem.intuition: We need the best possible sum from a continuous slice of the array.

Approach.why: Kadane's algorithm reduces O(n²) brute force to O(n) by reusing previous subarray sums.
Approach.what_if: Skipping this approach leads to inefficient nested loops that time out on large inputs.
Approach.intuition: At each step, decide if the current element alone is better than adding it to the previous subarray.

Pattern.why: Dynamic programming with a single state: the best sum ending at the current index.
Pattern.what_if: Ignoring the pattern might cause you to track all subarrays instead of just the running sum.
Pattern.intuition: The running sum is either the current element or the current element plus the previous running sum, whichever is larger.

Skeleton.why: Initialize two variables: current_sum and max_sum, then iterate once through the array.
Skeleton.what_if: Without a skeleton, you might forget to update max_sum or handle negative numbers correctly.
Skeleton.intuition: Start with first element, then for each next element, update current_sum and compare with max_sum.

Solution.why: Return max_sum after processing all elements; it holds the largest contiguous sum.
Solution.what_if: Returning the wrong variable (e.g., current_sum) gives the last subarray sum, not the global maximum.
Solution.intuition: The answer is the best sum we've seen at any point during the single pass.

Problem.why: Defines the exact goal: find the maximum product from any contiguous subarray.
Problem.what_if: Without a clear problem statement, you might solve for sum or non-contiguous subsets.
Problem.intuition: We need to scan the array and keep track of the best product seen so far.

Approach.why: A single negative can turn a large negative product into a large positive, so we must track both current max and min.
Approach.what_if: Tracking only max would miss cases where a negative flips a min into a new max.
Approach.intuition: At each step, the new max is the largest of (current number, current number * previous max, current number * previous min).

Pattern.why: This is a dynamic programming pattern where state depends on both max and min ending at each position.
Pattern.what_if: Using a greedy or single-variable approach would fail on arrays with negative numbers.
Pattern.intuition: We maintain two variables that update simultaneously, like juggling two balls.

Skeleton.why: Provides the structure: initialize variables, loop through array, update max/min, track global max.
Skeleton.what_if: Skipping initialization (e.g., setting max to 0) would break when all numbers are negative.
Skeleton.intuition: Start with the first element, then for each next element, decide how it changes the running products.

Solution.why: Implements the logic correctly, handling zeros and negatives by swapping max and min when current is negative.
Solution.what_if: Forgetting to swap when current is negative would use the wrong previous max/min for multiplication.
Solution.intuition: When you see a negative, the roles of max and min swap because multiplying flips the sign.

Problem.why: Defines the exact input/output and constraints (adjacent moves, no cell reuse).
Problem.what_if: Without a clear problem statement, you might solve a different puzzle (e.g., allowing diagonal moves or revisiting cells).
Problem.intuition: You need to find a path in a grid that spells the word, like a word search puzzle in a newspaper.

Approach.what_if: Skipping backtracking would force you to try all permutations of cells, which is exponentially slower and impractical.
Approach.intuition: It's like trying every possible route in a maze, but you stop and turn back as soon as you hit a dead end.

Pattern.why: The pattern of marking visited cells with a sentinel and restoring them prevents reusing cells in the current path.
Pattern.what_if: Without marking, you could loop infinitely or reuse a cell, giving false positives for words that require distinct cells.
Pattern.intuition: You temporarily 'block' a cell so you don't step on it again, like putting a 'do not enter' sign that you remove when you leave.

Skeleton.why: A skeleton (nested loops for start cells + recursive DFS) structures the solution cleanly.
Skeleton.what_if: Without a skeleton, the code becomes a tangled mess of loops and recursion, hard to debug or extend.
Skeleton.intuition: Think of it as a blueprint: first try every possible starting point, then for each, explore neighbors recursively.

Solution.why: The final code combines all parts: iterate over board, call DFS from each cell, return true if any path matches the word.
Solution.what_if: If the solution is wrong (e.g., missing boundary checks), you might get index errors or miss valid words.
Solution.intuition: The solution is the complete recipe: start at each cell, walk step by step, backtrack when stuck, and return success if you spell the whole word.

Problem.why: Identifies the core goal: counting distinct connected groups of '1's.
Problem.what_if: Without understanding connectivity, you might count singleton cells or miss merged groups.
Problem.intuition: Think of each '1' as a piece of land and islands as clusters that touch at edges.

Approach.why: Flood-fill ensures we traverse an entire island from any starting cell, marking it visited.
Approach.what_if: If not applied, you could count the same island multiple times or never fully explore it.
Approach.intuition: Like pouring water on one part of an island and watching it spread to cover the whole thing.

Pattern.why: DFS/BFS systematically visits all adjacent land cells, preventing redundant exploration.
Pattern.what_if: Without a traversal pattern, you might loop infinitely or miss neighbors, causing incorrect counts.
Pattern.intuition: Recursively or queue-based expand in four directions until no more land remains in that island.

Skeleton.why: Structures the code: loop over grid, on finding unvisited '1' increment count and flood-fill.
Skeleton.what_if: Skipping the outer loop means never discovering islands; skipping flood-fill means counting each cell separately.
Skeleton.intuition: The skeleton is the 'find one, erase entire island, repeat' pattern.

Solution.why: Combines the skeleton and traversal to produce the correct island count.
Solution.what_if: Wrong implementation (e.g., incorrect bounds check or marking) leads to under/overcounting.
Solution.intuition: Count is simply the number of times you start a fresh flood-fill over the whole grid.

Problem.why: Defines the input constraints and the goal of detecting if a valid course order exists.
Problem.what_if: Misunderstanding the problem could lead to solving the wrong graph problem (e.g., counting components instead of detecting cycles).
Problem.intuition: Think of courses as nodes and prerequisites as directed edges; we need to check if the graph has a cycle.

Approach.what_if: Using a simple visited set without tracking recursion stack would miss cycles that are not back edges to an ancestor.
Approach.intuition: We mark nodes as 'in progress' while exploring their dependencies; if we revisit one, it's a cycle.

Pattern.why: Cycle detection in a directed graph is a fundamental pattern for scheduling and dependency resolution.
Pattern.what_if: Confusing it with undirected cycle detection would incorrectly flag some valid DAGs as invalid.
Pattern.intuition: This is like checking if a prerequisite chain loops back on itself, making it impossible to start.

Skeleton.why: The skeleton provides the function signature and the adjacency list construction, which is the foundation for traversal.
Skeleton.what_if: Skipping adjacency list construction would make graph traversal O(n^2) or impossible to implement efficiently.
Skeleton.intuition: We need a map from each course to its list of prerequisites to know where to DFS from.

Solution.why: The solution implements DFS with three states (0=unvisited, 1=visiting, 2=visited) and returns False if a cycle is found.
Solution.what_if: Forgetting to mark nodes as fully visited after recursion would cause false cycle detections on subsequent DFS calls.
Solution.intuition: We traverse each unvisited course; if we ever see a node marked 'visiting', we have a cycle and cannot finish all courses.

Problem.why: Defines the exact task: deep copy a connected undirected graph from a given node.
Problem.what_if: Without a clear problem statement, you might attempt a shallow copy or miss the undirected nature.
Problem.intuition: Think of cloning a social network where each person and their friendships must be duplicated exactly.

Approach.why: DFS ensures we traverse every node exactly once while building the clone.
Approach.what_if: Using BFS or recursion without a visited map could cause infinite loops or missed nodes.
Approach.intuition: Like exploring a maze with a map to avoid revisiting dead ends.

Pattern.why: Hashmap from original to clone prevents duplicate cloning and cycles.
Pattern.what_if: Without the map, you'd reclone neighbors infinitely, causing stack overflow or incorrect graph.
Pattern.intuition: A dictionary acts as a 'memory' so each node is born only once.

Skeleton.why: Base case: if node is null, return null; if already cloned, return clone from map.
Skeleton.what_if: Missing base case leads to null pointer errors or infinite recursion.
Skeleton.intuition: Check if the node is already 'registered' before creating a new copy.

Solution.why: Create clone, store in map, then recursively clone all neighbors and attach.
Solution.what_if: Forgetting to store before recursing causes duplicate clones and cycles.
Solution.intuition: First make a copy of the person, then copy all their friends using the same rule.

Problem.why: Defines the goal: find cells whose water reaches both oceans.
Problem.what_if: Without a clear problem statement, you might solve the wrong direction or miss the dual-ocean requirement.
Problem.intuition: Think of each cell as a potential source that must connect to two different sinks.

Approach.what_if: Starting from every interior cell would be O((mn)^2) and time out on large grids.

Approach.why: Building a trie first lets us prune the search by only following prefixes that exist in any target word.
Approach.what_if: Skipping the trie forces a separate DFS per word, which is O(N * M * 4^L) and extremely slow for many words.
Approach.intuition: The trie acts like a shared map so we don't waste time exploring dead ends that no word can complete.

Pattern.why: Backtracking with a trie is the classic pattern for multi-word search on a grid, combining prefix sharing with depth-first exploration.
Pattern.what_if: Using a naive set of words without a trie would still require checking each word individually, losing the benefit of common prefixes.
Pattern.intuition: We walk the board and the trie simultaneously, backtracking when the current path is not a prefix of any word.
